title: {{NAME}} and the League of Extraordinary Creatures
moral: Every kind of strength matters, and the bravest thing you can do is offer yours when it is needed.

pages.content:
The signal appeared at midnight: a beam of silver light rising from the rooftop of the old clock tower, shaped like a compass pointing in four directions at once. {{NAME}} had been waiting for exactly this, though he had not known he was waiting until the moment he saw it.

By the time he reached the clock tower's roof, the others were already there. A golden eagle named Vance, who wore a sleek red visor and had the focused stillness of someone who could see for fifty kilometres in every direction. A river otter named Pip, whose quicksilver speed was matched only by her inability to sit still for more than four consecutive seconds. And a great grey tortoise named Aldric, who was very old, very slow, and possessed of a power so formidable that even Vance treated him with particular respect: he could predict, with absolute precision, where any danger would arrive and exactly when.

Aldric looked at {{NAME}} over the rim of his magnificent shell and said, with the unhurried certainty of someone who had known this moment was coming for forty years: 'You're the last piece. We leave in six minutes. I suggest you stretch your legs.'

pages.content:
Aldric had predicted that a dam in the valley would begin to fail at precisely 2:47 in the morning. Not might fail. Would fail. The old tortoise had been wrong approximately once in four decades, and that time he had simply been thirteen minutes early.

Flying to the valley took eight minutes with Vance carrying {{NAME}} in his great talons, the wind a roar in {{NAME}}'s ears and the city lights spreading below them like scattered embers. Pip shot alongside at water level, her small body a silver streak. Aldric, they had left behind. There are some things a tortoise cannot meaningfully help with in real time, but his instructions had been precise and clear and {{NAME}} had memorised every word.

{{NAME}}'s face in the rushing night air was all focus and bright-eyed readiness, his purple cape streaming behind him like a banner. Fear was there too, small and honest, sitting in the corner of his chest. He did not push it away. It was just another part of being ready.

pages.content:
The dam was a curving wall of stone and concrete above a sleeping valley. Even from the air {{NAME}} could see it: a thin fracture line spreading from a point two-thirds up the dam face, growing, slowly but without pause.

Aldric's instructions played through {{NAME}}'s head in perfect order. The emergency release valve was on the eastern face, twelve metres up, accessible by a maintenance ladder. Opening it would reduce the pressure before the fracture spread, but the valve wheel required more force than one person could provide. This was the part Aldric had smiled about.

Pip was already on the ladder before Vance touched down, her otter hands perfectly adapted to the wet metal rungs. {{NAME}} climbed behind her at full speed. Together, Pip pushing from below and {{NAME}} pulling from above, the wheel turned, groaned, resisted, and then surrendered.

The water came through the release channel in a controlled white rush, exactly where it was supposed to go. The fracture stopped spreading. The valley stayed asleep, unknowing and safe.

pages.content:
Aldric was waiting on the clock tower roof when they returned, which was not a surprise. His expression when they landed was exactly the same as when they had left: measured, calm, deeply satisfied.

'2:44,' he said. 'Three minutes early. You made good time.'

Pip collapsed dramatically onto her back on the rooftop tiles, paws in the air, and made a long, elaborate sound of exhausted triumph. Vance landed with the precision of a machine and folded his wings without comment. {{NAME}} sat down heavily beside Aldric, breathing hard, heart still hammering.

Aldric laid one ancient grey flipper very gently on {{NAME}}'s arm. 'The compass,' he said, nodding at the silver emblem on {{NAME}}'s chest, 'points in four directions. Four is not a coincidence.' His old eyes were warm. 'Each of you carried exactly what was needed. Not more. Not less. That is how it always works, when it works.'

{{NAME}} looked at his three companions in the dark and felt something bloom in his chest that had no clean name but felt like belonging.

pages.content:
The clock tower struck three, and the city below was peaceful and whole and completely unaware of what had happened above it while it slept.

Pip righted herself and curled into a neat, quick ball against {{NAME}}'s side, warm as a small living sun. Vance perched on the parapet and resumed his watch over the world, which he would maintain until dawn without complaint or fatigue. Aldric closed his ancient eyes.

{{NAME}} leaned back against the cool stone of the tower and looked up at the stars. His cape pooled around him like a purple lake. Somewhere in the valley, the dam stood solid. Somewhere in the city, four hundred families slept without knowing that three animals and one boy had stood in the dark and done something necessary and quiet and brave.

His eyes fell closed, and the city's soft hum became the sound of dreaming.

Goodnight, compass-heart. Rest well, and wonder what signal the next clear night might bring.
